title: Buckets: S3 for runs
bridge: An S3 bucket is like a huge key-value store where each key looks like a file path. Except there are no real folders, only key prefixes. Who may read or write is decided by IAM and endpoint policies together. A presigned URL is like a one-time download link: whoever holds it can use it until it expires.
intro: A VM is a workbench we throw away, so everything a run must keep lives in S3. That means its transcript, notes and artifacts. This lesson builds the runs bucket with encryption, blocked public access, versioning and a 30-day expiry. Then it shows how a VM with no AWS keys still reads and writes it.

picture.caption: The broker signs a short link for one key and the VM uses it over plain HTTP. S3 encrypts, and deletes after 30 days.

nodes.label: nova-worker in the VM (no AWS keys)

steps.text: POST /v1/artifacts/url {name, write}: asks for a link to its own prefix
signs a 15-minute PUT for runs/<run_id>/<name> with its own role
PUTs the object with fetch; the endpoint allows only our buckets
the request reaches the bucket without leaving AWS
S3 encrypts the object with the bucket's own key
after 30 days the rule deletes objects under runs/

sections.h: Start: a bucket and a key
p: A bucket is a named container for objects. An object is bytes plus a key, its name. The key runs/run-42/notes.md looks like a path, but S3 has no folders: runs/run-42/ is a prefix, the start of many keys.

Bucket names are global across all of AWS, which is why ours carries rhino in front. G3-04 creates rhino-ai-agents-runs in the ai-agents account. Every run writes under runs/<run_id>/, and its session transcript under runs/<run_id>/sessions/ (G3-23).
sections.because: We make the bucket and one object by hand first, so the settings in the next sections have something to act on.

code.text:
aws s3api create-bucket --bucket rhino-ai-agents-runs
echo "plan approved by Sean" > notes.md
aws s3 cp notes.md s3://rhino-ai-agents-runs/runs/run-42/notes.md
aws s3 ls s3://rhino-ai-agents-runs/runs/run-42/

notes.text: In us-east-1 no location setting is needed. Elsewhere you add --create-bucket-configuration.
The key is runs/run-42/notes.md. The s3:// form is the CLI's shorthand for bucket plus key.
Lists keys that start with the prefix, as if it were a folder.

p: S3 can encrypt every object at rest with a key from KMS, AWS's key service. That is SSE-KMS: server-side encryption with KMS. With our own key, its key policy decides who may decrypt, on top of bucket access.

G3-04 gives the runs bucket its own KMS key. A bucket key setting makes S3 ask KMS less often, which keeps costs and throttling down. After this, every new object is encrypted without the writer doing anything.
sections.because: We use our own key because 'who may decrypt' should be one key policy we control, not AWS's default key.

code.text:
KEY=$(aws kms create-key --description "runs bucket" --query KeyMetadata.Arn --output text)
aws s3api put-bucket-encryption --bucket rhino-ai-agents-runs \
  --server-side-encryption-configuration "{\"Rules\":[{\"ApplyServerSideEncryptionByDefault\":{\"SSEAlgorithm\":\"aws:kms\",\"KMSMasterKeyID\":\"$KEY\"},\"BucketKeyEnabled\":true}]}"
aws s3 cp notes.md s3://rhino-ai-agents-runs/runs/run-42/notes.md
aws s3api head-object --bucket rhino-ai-agents-runs --key runs/run-42/notes.md \
  --query '[ServerSideEncryption,SSEKMSKeyId]' --output text

notes.text: A new KMS key. In G3-04 it is a Terraform resource with a key policy.
Default encryption: aws:kms with our key, and the bucket key on.
Upload again: only objects written after the setting are encrypted with it.
head-object reads an object's settings without downloading it.

p: Block Public Access is four switches that stop any ACL (an old per-object permission list) or bucket policy from making data public. G3-04 turns all four on. Even a mistaken policy later cannot open the bucket.

Versioning keeps every version of a key. An overwrite or a delete keeps the old version. A bad write by a run is not the end of its work. Old versions cost storage, so the next section cleans them up.
sections.because: We block public access at the bucket because a run's transcript may quote code and tickets. A single wrong setting must not expose it.

code.text:
aws s3api put-public-access-block --bucket rhino-ai-agents-runs \
  --public-access-block-configuration \
  BlockPublicAcls=true,IgnorePublicAcls=true,BlockPublicPolicy=true,RestrictPublicBuckets=true
aws s3api put-bucket-versioning --bucket rhino-ai-agents-runs \
  --versioning-configuration Status=Enabled
aws s3api get-bucket-versioning --bucket rhino-ai-agents-runs --output text

notes.text: Refuse public ACLs, ignore any that exist, refuse public policies, and limit access if one slips in.
Once enabled, versioning can only be suspended, never fully turned off.
Prints Enabled. trivy (p4-6) flags buckets without these settings.

p: A lifecycle rule tells S3 to act on objects by age. G3-04 keeps transcripts 30 days, then they go. The Agent SDK never deletes from a session store, so this rule is the only retention (G3-23).

With versioning on, Expiration does not erase data. It adds a delete marker, and the old version stays as a noncurrent version. A second action, NoncurrentVersionExpiration, removes those. The ticket names only the 30 days; agree the noncurrent number with DevOps.
sections.because: We expire runs in S3 itself because nobody should have to remember to clean up a bucket.

notes.text: Rules can be switched off without deleting them.
Only keys under runs/. Other prefixes keep their own rules.
30 days after an object is written, it gets a delete marker.
One day after a version stops being current, it is deleted for good. The 1 is our choice.

p: A presigned URL is a request signed in advance. The broker signs it with its own role's credentials (G3-17), for one operation on one key, with an expiry. Whoever holds the URL can do exactly that until it expires, with no AWS keys at all.
G3-13 gives the broker POST /v1/artifacts/url: 15-minute PUT or GET links for runs/<run_id>/<name> only. The harness then uploads with fetch. Below is the same signing call, outside the broker.
sections.because: We presign because the VM must save its work, and the VM holds no credentials.

notes.text: forcePathStyle puts the bucket in the path, which moto needs. Real S3 works either way.
The key is always under this run's prefix. The broker also cleans the name (safeName in G3-13).
Builds the URL locally: no request is sent. 900 seconds is G3-13's 15 minutes.
The URL carries the signature, the expiry and the signer's key ID, never the secret.

p: The broker's role may put and get objects under runs/* only (G3-17). It is the only identity that signs links. The S3 gateway endpoint allows only our buckets (p3-2). A link to someone else's bucket fails from inside the sandbox VPC.
A link names one key and dies after 15 minutes. If one leaks into a log, the damage is one object for a few minutes. The VM never sees a key that could list, read or delete anything else.

callout.text: No keys in the VM. The harness asks the broker for each link; the broker decides which run may touch which prefix.

quiz.q: A sandbox VM has no AWS keys. How does it upload its transcript?

options.text: It reads the instance role's credentials from IMDS and calls S3
options.why: The role holds no S3 permission, and the agent cannot reach IMDS anyway (p3-3).

options.text: It asks the broker for a presigned PUT URL for its own prefix, then uploads with fetch
options.why: The broker signs; the VM only holds a short-lived link to one key.

options.text: It sends the file through the proxy to s3.amazonaws.com with the broker's key
options.why: The broker's key never leaves the broker, and S3 goes through the endpoint, not the proxy.

quiz.q: Versioning is on. What does a 30-day Expiration rule do to an object?

options.text: Deletes every version of it at once
options.why: Expiration on a versioned bucket only adds a delete marker.

options.text: Adds a delete marker; old versions stay until a noncurrent-version rule removes them
options.why: That is why the lesson adds NoncurrentVersionExpiration.

options.text: Nothing: lifecycle rules do not work on versioned buckets
options.why: They work; they act differently on current and noncurrent versions.

quiz.q: Someone copies a presigned GET URL out of a log. What can they do with it?

options.why: A presigned URL is for one operation on one key.

options.text: Nothing: presigned URLs only work from the sandbox VPC
options.why: A presigned URL is a bearer link. Our endpoint policy limits what leaves the VPC, not who can use a link.

options.text: Read that one object until the link expires, 15 minutes after signing
options.why: That small, short window is why links are scoped and short.

recall: From p3-2: why does the S3 gateway endpoint policy list our buckets and nothing else?

words.plain: A named container for objects in S3; names are unique across all of AWS.
An object's name, like runs/run-42/notes.md; a prefix is the start shared by many keys.
S3 encrypting objects at rest with a KMS key; ours has its own key and key policy.
Four bucket switches that stop any ACL or policy from making data public.
S3 keeps every version of a key, so overwrites and deletes keep the old data.
A bucket rule that expires or moves objects by age, such as 30 days under runs/.
A link signed in advance for one operation on one key, usable by anyone until it expires.

tickets.why: Creates rhino-ai-agents-runs with its own KMS key, public access blocked, versioning and a 30-day expiry.
The broker's POST /v1/artifacts/url: 15-minute presigned PUT or GET for the run's own prefix only.
The session store writes transcript parts under runs/<run_id>/sessions/ through presigned URLs.

remember: A run keeps its work in one encrypted, private bucket under runs/<run_id>/. It gets there through 15-minute links the broker signs, and S3 deletes it after 30 days.
